problems.fact: A recorder may use proprietary compression inside WAV; Audacity recommends its FFmpeg library for such imports.
Very large recordings may require RF64 rather than the original RIFF size fields.
Metadata handling varies: standard INFO chunks and Broadcast WAVE extensions store different information.

background.fact: WAVE is a RIFF-based wrapper for sound, rather than one particular audio encoding.
Microsoft and IBM documented the format in their August 1991 multimedia specification.
Linear PCM is a common WAVE payload, but compressed encodings can appear too.
The usual filename ending is .wav; audio/wav and audio/x-wav are common media-type labels.
Broadcast WAVE extends the format with metadata for production and preservation.
The Library of Congress recommends WAVE for digital audio collections.

problems.fact: An editor can recognize AVI but still lack the decoder needed for its particular contents.
Original AVI size restrictions differ from the later OpenDML extension; large captures need compatible software.
Aspect ratio and scan-type metadata are not handled consistently across AVI implementations.

background.fact: AVI carries timed pictures and sound inside a RIFF file.
Microsoft introduced AVI with Windows 3.1, and its first specification dates to 1992.
FOURCC identifiers describe the streams and their codecs.
The header records properties such as dimensions and frame rate; another chunk stores the media.
AVI can wrap uncompressed, lossless, or lossy video, so the extension alone does not identify quality.
Files normally end in .avi; video/x-msvideo is one commonly used media-type label.
AVI appears in video production archives and older desktop video workflows.
TIFF is a tag-based raster wrapper developed by Aldus and Microsoft.
TIFF revision 6.0 was published in 1992, and Adobe now controls its specification.
A TIFF can use different compression methods and different color representations.
The extensions .tif and .tiff refer to this format, with the media type image/tiff.
TIFF can contain multiple images, making it useful for scanned document sequences.
High-bit-depth imaging and preservation master files are established TIFF uses.

problems.fact: Classic TIFF uses 32-bit offsets, which constrain size to about 4 GB; BigTIFF extends those fields.
A reader may not understand every private tag, including some color-profile extensions.
A TIFF may hold several images; use software that exposes the full image sequence.

problems.fact: Choosing the wrong audio or subtitle stream can give the wrong language; mpv provides track selection controls.
Missing or damaged cues can make seeking harder; Matroska defines cues separately from the media clusters.
Container recognition does not ensure every embedded codec can be decoded by the chosen player.

background.fact: Matroska is an audiovisual container built on EBML, a binary structure derived from XML.
The format developed from the earlier MCF project.
A Matroska file can carry several video, audio, and subtitle streams.
Chapters and descriptive tags are part of its design.
The container does not prescribe one compression method or a fixed level of quality.
IANA registers video/matroska for Matroska video.
